counterexample: Take m = 5, n = 4, so S = {5, 6, 7, 8}. Line 0025 asserts the n elements of S can be written as k_1*1, k_2*2, k_3*3, k_4*4 with the factors 1,2,3,4 attached to DISTINCT elements. Here 4 must be matched to 8 (the only multiple of 4), 3 must be matched to 6 (the only multiple of 3), and then 2 has no remaining even element (6 and 8 are used, 5 and 7 are odd). So no such factorization of the product 5*6*7*8 into k_1 * 2k_2 * 3k_3 * 4k_4 with the k_i coming from a one-to-one assignment of the elements exists, even though 4! = 24 does divide 1680. The proof's central identity therefore fails; the theorem itself is still true.
